The office is the prominent thought in the latter arrangement; the person, in the former. He here marks the Messiahship of "Christ," maintained by him as the origin of his being a "prisoner," owing to the jealousy of the Jews being roused at his preaching it to the Gentiles. His very bonds were profitable to ("for" or "in behalf of you") Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.13">Ep 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.10">2Ti 2:10</reference>). entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 3 Ep 3:1-21 . His Apostolic Office to Make Known the Mystery of Christ Revealed by the Spirit: Prayer that by the Same Spirit They May Comprehend the Vast Love of Christ: Doxology Ending This Division of the Epistle. As the first chapter treated of THE Father's office; and the second, THE Son's, so this, that of THE Spirit. 1. of Jesus Christ-- Greek, "Christ Jesus." The office is the prominent thought in the latter arrangement; the person, in the former. He here marks the Messiahship of "Christ," maintained by him as the origin of his being a "prisoner," owing to the jealousy of the Jews being roused at his preaching it to the Gentiles. His very bonds were profitable to ("for" or "in behalf of you") Gentiles ( Ep 3:13 ; 2Ti 2:10 ). He digresses at "For this cause," and does not complete the sentence which he had intended, until Ep 3:14 , where he resumes the words, "For this cause," namely, because I know this your call of God as Gentiles ( Ep 2:11-22 ), to be "fellow-heirs" with the Jews ( Ep 3:6 ), "I bow my knees to" the Father of our common Saviour ( Ep 3:14 , 15 ) to confirm you in the faith by His Spirit. "I Paul," expresses the agent employed by the Spirit to enlighten them, after he had been first enlightened himself by the same Spirit (Ep 3:3-5, 9).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17617"/><div sID="gen35524" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17617"/><hi type="bold">2. If--</hi>The Greek does not imply doubt: "Assuming (what I know to be the fact, namely) that ye have heard," &c. "If, as I presume," The indicative in the Greek shows that no doubt is implied: "Seeing that doubtless," &c. He by this phrase delicately reminds them of their having heard from himself, and probably from others subsequently, the fact. See Introduction, showing that these words do not disprove the address of this Epistle to the Ephesians. Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.20.17-Acts.20.24">Ac 20:17-24</reference>.<div eID="gen35524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the dispensation--</hi>"The office of dispensing, as a steward, the grace of God which was (not 'is') given me to you-ward," namely, to dispense to you. <div eID="gen35525" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17620"/><div sID="gen35530" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17620"/><hi type="bold">5. in other ages--</hi>Greek, "generations."<div eID="gen35530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not made known--</hi>He does not say, "has not been revealed." Making known by revelation is the source of making known by preaching [Bengel]. The former was vouchsafed only to the prophets, in order that they might make known the truth so revealed to men in general.<div eID="gen35531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35532" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the sons of men--</hi>men in their state by birth, as contrasted with those illuminated "by the Spirit" (Greek, "IN the Spirit," compare <reference osisRef="Rev.1.10">Re 1:10</reference>), <reference osisRef="Matt.16.17">Mt 16:17</reference>.<div eID="gen35532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as--</hi>The mystery of the call of the Gentiles (of which Paul speaks here) was not unknown to the Old Testament prophets (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.6">Is 56:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.6">49:6</reference>). But they did not know it with the same explicit distinctness "As" it has been now known (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.19">Ac 10:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.11.18-Acts.11.21">11:18-21</reference>). They probably did not know that the Gentiles were to be admitted without circumcision or that they were to be on a level with the Jews in partaking of the grace of God. The gift of "the Spirit" in its fulness was reserved for the New Testament that Christ might thereby be glorified. The epithet, "holy," marks the special consecration of the New Testament "prophets" (who are here meant) by the Spirit, compared with which even the Old Testament prophets were but "sons of men" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.2.3">Eze 2:3</reference>, and elsewhere). <div eID="gen35533" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17621"/><div sID="gen35534" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17621"/>6. Translate, "That the Gentiles are," &c. "and fellow members of the same body, and fellow partakers of the (so the oldest manuscripts read, not 'His') promise, in Christ Jesus (added in the oldest manuscripts), through the Gospel." It is "in Christ Jesus" that they are made "fellow heirs" in the inheritance of God: "of the same body" under the Head, Christ Jesus; and "fellow partakers of the promise" in the communion of THE Holy Spirit (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">Ep 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.4">He 6:4</reference>). The Trinity is thus alluded to, as often elsewhere in this Epistle (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.19">Ep 2:19</reference>, 20, 22). <div eID="gen35534" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17624"/><div sID="gen35542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17624"/><hi type="bold">9. to make all men see--</hi>Greek, "to enlighten all" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Ep 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.28">Psa 18:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.4">He 6:4</reference>). "All" (compare <reference osisRef="Col.1.28">Col 1:28</reference>).<div eID="gen35542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fellowship--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "economy," or "dispensation" (compare <reference osisRef="Col.1.25">Col 1:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26">26</reference>; and see on <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference>, above). "To make all see how it hath seemed good to God at this time to dispense (through me and others, His stewards) what heretofore was a mystery." Ellicott explains it, "the arrangement," or "regulation" of the mystery (the union of Jews and Gentiles in Christ) which was now to be humbly traced and acknowledged in the fact of its having secretly existed in the counsel of God, and now having been revealed to the heavenly powers by means of the Church.<div eID="gen35543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the beginning of the world--</hi>Greek, "from (the beginning of) the ages." Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25">Ro 16:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Co 2:7</reference>. The "ages" are the vast successive periods of time, marked by successive stages of creation and orders of beings.<div eID="gen35544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in God--</hi>"hidden in" His counsels (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.9">Ep 1:9</reference>).<div eID="gen35545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">created all things by Jesus Christ--</hi>God's creation of the world and all things therein is the foundation of the rest of the "economy," which is freely dispensed according to the universal power of God [Bengel]. AS God created "the whole range of things" (so the Greek), physical and spiritual alike, He must have an absolute right to adjust all things as He will. Hence, we may see His right to keep the mystery of world-wide salvation in Christ "hidden in Himself," till his own good time for revealing it. The oldest manuscripts omit "by Jesus Christ." <div eID="gen35546" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17630"/><div sID="gen35562" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17630"/><hi type="bold">15. the whole family--</hi>Alford, Middleton, and others translate, "every family": alluding to the several families in heaven and in earth supposed to exist [Theophylact, Æcumenius, in Suicer, 2.633], the apostle thus being supposed to imply that God, in His relation of Father to us His adopted children, is the great prototype of the paternal relation wherever found. But the idea that "the holy angels are bound up in spiritual families or compaternities," is nowhere else in Scripture referred to. And <reference osisRef="Acts.2.36">Ac 2:36</reference>, where the article is similarly omitted, and yet the translation is, "All the house of Israel," shows that in New Testament Greek the translation is justifiable, "all the family," or "the whole family": which accords with Scripture views, that angels and men, the saints militant and those with God, are one holy family joined under the one Father in Christ, the mediator between heaven and earth (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.10">Php 2:10</reference>). Hence angels are termed our "brethren" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.10">Re 19:10</reference>), and "sons of God" by creation, as we are by adoption (<reference osisRef="Job.38.7">Job 38:7</reference>). The Church is part of the grand family, or kingdom, which comprehends, besides men, the higher spiritual world, where the archetype, to the realization of which redeemed man is now tending, is already realized. This universal idea of the "kingdom" of God as one divine community, is presented to us in the Lord's Prayer. By sin men were estranged, not only from God, but from that higher spiritual world in which the kingdom of God is already realized. As Christ when He reconciled men to God, united them to one another in a divine community (joined to Himself, the one Head), breaking down the partition wall between Jew and Gentile (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Ep 2:14</reference>), so also He joins them in communion with all those who have already attained that perfection in the kingdom of God, to which the Church on earth is aspiring (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>) [Neander].<div eID="gen35562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35563" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is named--</hi>derives its origin and its name as sons of God. To be named, and to be, are one with God. To bear God's name is to belong to God as His own peculiar people (<reference osisRef="Num.6.27">Nu 6:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.7">Is 43:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">44:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.25">Ro 9:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.26">26</reference>). <div eID="gen35563" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17633"/><div sID="gen35571" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17633"/><hi type="bold">18. May be able--</hi>even still further. Greek, "May be fully able."<div eID="gen35571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breadth ... length ... depth ... height--</hi>namely, the full dimensions of the spiritual temple, answering to "the fulness of God" (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.19">Ep 3:19</reference>), to which the Church, according to its capacity, ought to correspond (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.4.10">Ep 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.13">13</reference>) as to "the fulness of Christ." The "breadth" implies Christ's world-wide love, embracing all men: the "length," its being extended through all ages (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.21">Ep 3:21</reference>); the "depth," its profound wisdom which no creature can fathom (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Ro 11:33</reference>); the "height," its being beyond the reach of any foe to deprive us of (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Ep 4:8</reference>) [Bengel]. I prefer to understand "the breadth," &c., to refer to the whole of the vast mystery of free salvation in Christ for all, Gentile and Jew alike, of which Paul had been speaking (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.3-Eph.3.9">Ep 3:3-9</reference>), and of which he now prays they may have a fuller comprehension. As subsidiary to this, and the most essential part of it, he adds, "and to know the love of Christ" (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.19">Ep 3:19</reference>). Grotius understands depth and height of God's goodness raising us from the lowest depression to the greatest height. <div eID="gen35572" type="x-p"/>

As subsidiary to this, and the most essential part of it, he adds, "and to know the love of Christ" ( Ep 3:19 ). Grotius understands depth and height of God's goodness raising us from the lowest depression to the greatest height.
entries.reader_content_plain: 18. May be able-- even still further. Greek, "May be fully able." breadth ... length ... depth ... height-- namely, the full dimensions of the spiritual temple, answering to "the fulness of God" ( Ep 3:19 ), to which the Church, according to its capacity, ought to correspond (compare Ep 4:10 , 13 ) as to "the fulness of Christ." The "breadth" implies Christ's world-wide love, embracing all men: the "length," its being extended through all ages ( Ep 3:21 ); the "depth," its profound wisdom which no creature can fathom ( Ro 11:33 ); the "height," its being beyond the reach of any foe to deprive us of ( Ep 4:8 ) [Bengel]. I prefer to understand "the breadth," &c., to refer to the whole of the vast mystery of free salvation in Christ for all, Gentile and Jew alike, of which Paul had been speaking ( Ep 3:3-9 ), and of which he now prays they may have a fuller comprehension. As subsidiary to this, and the most essential part of it, he adds, "and to know the love of Christ" ( Ep 3:19 ). Grotius understands depth and height of God's goodness raising us from the lowest depression to the greatest height.
